column2: The person he consulted was none other than Wang. “This is my first attempt at naming a business,” Wang laughed. “I don't even know how to begin. What are the requirements?” “First, it must sound impressive and be easy to say. Second, the characters must be distinctive, so nobody confuses it with another firm. Naturally, it must suit a bank and be auspicious.” “Very well. Let me think.” He was rather at a loss. Taking a book at random, he intended to select a few characters, write them down, and then try different combinations. The volume he pulled from the shelf was the Chronicles of Huayang. He opened it and read a few lines. By a fortunate coincidence, two characters lay ready to hand. “What about these?” He wrote out a passage: “The age is peaceful, the way well governed; the people and their possessions flourish in abundance and well-being.” He circled the characters fu and kang. “Fukang, Fukang!” Hu repeated the name twice, then answered gladly, “Excellent! Both abundance and well-being. That's the one.”

As Hu rose to leave, Wang called him back. “Xueyan, I have news. I'm to receive a regular appointment.” “Oh! Which department or county?” “I don't know yet. Liu Er from the governor's office came to say that Governor Huang wishes to see me this evening. He let the news slip. I suppose it is time I received a post.” Just then a figure hurried past the window. Hu's sharp eyes recognised him. “It's Commissioner Wu.” The curtain lifted to reveal a smiling face. As Wu stepped inside, he saluted and announced loudly, “Congratulations, Your Honour! Wonderful news!” Wang paused, then understood. Wu had connections at the provincial treasury and must have heard of the appointment. He stood and repeatedly clasped his hands. “Thank you!” “I've just come from the treasurer's office,” Wu said, stepping closer. “The news is certain: you are to act as prefect of Huzhou.” Even Hu, who knew comparatively little of official practice, was astonished. An expectant department or county magistrate, who had not served a single day in a regular post of his own grade, was suddenly to leap to an acting prefecture? Surely that was extraordinary. Wang found it still harder to believe. “That... that doesn't sound quite right.” “There can be no mistake! The appointment will be posted tomorrow.”

Wang considered, still feeling that something was strange. He begged Wu to inquire further and sent Gao to ask Liu Er, who might have definite information. The news was both abrupt and intensely exciting. Torn between hope and fear, Wang could neither sit nor stand comfortably in his office. Hu urged him to remain calm. “Even if it isn't a prefecture, it must be a large county. You'll know when you see the governor tonight.” “I was thinking...” Wang's answer followed his own thoughts. “I paid little attention to what the treasurer said the other day. Now it seems significant.” “What did he say?” “First, that Huzhou's prefect had been dismissed for delaying the grain and that no replacement could be found. Then he said he had an idea, but immediately rejected it, muttering that it wouldn't work, that there was no precedent. Could it be connected with this news?” “Then that explains it!” Hu slapped his thigh. “Either the treasurer recommended you and the governor agreed, or the governor proposed it and the treasurer was happy to oblige. Let's hear what Liu Er tells Gao. If the treasurer has just been to see the governor, the news is eight-tenths certain.” “That makes sense.” Wang was greatly reassured.

“But remember, Mr Xuexuan: Huzhou has a great many powerful households. Its affairs are very difficult.” “Exactly! That's why you must still help me and come with me.” Hu could not agree to that. He put it aside for the moment. “We can discuss it later. There's another matter we must guard against. What happens to your assignment here?” “Here” meant the Sea Transport Bureau. The question reminded Wang of all that handing over its executive directorship would involve: the deficit must be made good and every affair under his management explained. A successor would have his own methods. If the bureau's funds ceased to be deposited with Xinhe and the relationship ended, their guarantee for the Songjiang association's loan could create serious trouble. It was indeed a danger to consider. “Yes!” Wang drew a breath. “A great deal depends on that. We must act early. I think I should tell the governor frankly and ask to retain the bureau as an additional duty. But if he says I couldn't manage provincial-capital business from Huzhou, we'll be in considerable difficulty.” “Then let me ask you this. If you reach the point where you can't have both, what will you choose?” “I'd rather decline the regular appointment and preserve our position here. I owe my present standing to my friends' help. I can't leave a burden that harms you, Zhang, and You.” Hu nodded deeply and spoke word by word. “With that principle, you'll never lack friends.” Having clarified his ultimate position, Wang felt calmer.

They discussed how he should address Huang under various circumstances. After about an hour, Gao returned. As Hu had expected, Huang had specially summoned Lingui that morning for a private consultation. Wu's news plainly had a basis. Soon Wu himself brought fuller confirmation: Wang was to act as magistrate of Wucheng County and concurrently as prefect of Huzhou. There could be no further doubt. Everyone at the bureau had heard and came together to congratulate their director. They also discussed subscribing for a feast and theatrical performance in his honour. Wang thought this far too ostentatious and firmly refused. He asked Wu to thank them and make absolutely clear that no such celebration should be held. Half a day of commotion produced no agreement. At last he put the matter aside and went punctually to the governor's summons.

“We must find a way to collect this year's full revenue. Military expenses are enormous. Ministry dispatches demanding remittances to the capital arrive one after another. Look—another edict.” Wang rose and took the document from Huang. Its lengthy text concerned raising military funds and encouraging contributions. The final passage read: “As provincial appropriations have failed to arrive on schedule, the Board of Revenue proposes suspending salary payments for one year, according to rank. We consider that princes and senior ministers have long enjoyed generous emoluments, so a temporary suspension is practicable. For civil officials below the fourth rank and military officials below the third, however, let the Board pay in full the salaries withheld this spring. Let five hundred thousand taels also be released from the privy treasury into the Board's treasury to meet essential salary and military expenditure.” Would princes and senior ministers tolerate a prolonged interruption of their salaries? Naturally, the provinces would face relentless demands for funds. Wang took warning: this year, local officials must give revenue collection precedence over everything. “Our province depends on Hangzhou, Jiaxing, and Huzhou, with Huzhou its particular lifeblood,” Huang continued. “Treasurer Lin and I have agreed that you must go. In this crisis, unparalleled in two hundred years, the court has repeatedly urged practical results and exceptional appointments where necessary. I therefore doubt it will reject my recommendation that you act as prefect.” Wang was prepared. As soon as Huang paused, he rose and saluted. “Such favour overwhelms me with gratitude and apprehension. I don't know how to repay it.” “Handle the public business properly, and that will be repayment enough. Huzhou is unlike other places, Brother Xuexuan. You must bring all your ability to bear.” “Yes. But there is a personal difficulty for which I must ask your special consideration.” “Speak. Anything that benefits the public business can be accommodated.”

“It concerns the Sea Transport Bureau. I've only recently taken charge. Your Excellency understands every complication of the official-procurement arrangement. Matters are still unfinished. If a successor, unaware of the circumstances, objects at every turn, then even apart from possible financial liabilities, the correspondence needed to explain and justify everything would consume enormous time. With me in Huzhou, how could I devote my full attention to revenue collection? I venture to ask you to remove this concern.” “What would you have me do?” “Allow me to hand over only after this affair has been concluded.” Huang fell silent, gazing into space as though calculating. Wang tried to read his thoughts. Had the post already been promised to someone else? “There is no objection in principle to your holding both duties,” Huang said slowly, bringing his eyes back to Wang. “But can you manage them?” The question was expected. “Rest assured, I can. I have an exceptionally capable man under me. Without his work in making contacts and negotiating on every side, the procurement affair could never have proceeded so smoothly.”

“Oh? What is his name? What qualifications does he hold? Bring him to see me sometime.” “His name is Hu Guangyong. He is young, and though a man of commerce, he has extraordinary abilities. At present he holds no official or scholarly qualification, so it may not be proper for him to seek an audience.” “That doesn't matter. There is much to be done. A talented man need not fear being overlooked. What business is he in?” “He...” Wang exaggerated on Hu's behalf. “He comes from a prosperous banking family and has now established a bank of his own.” “A bank? Good. Very good indeed!” The repeated approval had a strange tone. Wang feared some concealed implication and grew watchful. “Speaking of banks reminds me of something,” Huang continued. “Senior officials in the capital and governors throughout the provinces are contributing to military funds. I too must make an effort. I intend to assemble ten thousand taels as a modest contribution. In a few days, ask this Mr Hu's bank to remit it for me.” “Certainly. We should be honoured to serve. Please send the money whenever convenient.”

At that, Huang lifted his tea bowl, signalling the end of the audience. Nothing further was said about retaining the bureau. Wang was anxious. Left suspended between possibilities, he could not see how to obtain a definite answer. As soon as he left, he sent Gao to find Hu. Hu arrived just after him. Without even changing his clothes, Wang took him into the study, closed the door, and recounted everything. “The bureau is now hanging in mid-air. I don't know where to begin. Isn't that maddening? If he'd simply refused, I could have stated my decision. As it is, I can neither advance nor retreat.” “Never mind. It's very easy,” Hu said casually. “A little more silver will settle it.” “Why, I don't believe you! How can you be so sure? And how much is ‘a little’? How would it be spent?” “Mr Xuexuan, you're clever all your life and muddled for a moment. He's already named his price: ten thousand taels.” “Ah!” Wang understood. “No wonder!” He reconsidered the scene. Because he had failed to grasp the implication, he had asked Huang to send the money at his convenience. Hearing that he had missed the point, Huang had immediately dismissed him. The abrupt coldness was disheartening.

“No more talk. Act quickly. The right medicine cures the illness; there's no reason to delay.” “Certainly.” Wang considered. “Tomorrow I'll have Xinhe remit ten thousand to the ministry.” “Wait. Give me that money. I have another use for it.” The words were puzzling, but Wang did not ask. Showing complete trust was one of his methods of securing Hu's loyalty. He nodded. “Come to the bureau tomorrow morning to collect it.” “No. You'll be very busy. I won't disturb you. Send the draft to me, and I'll finish the business during the morning. We'll meet at noon.” “Wait, let me think.” Wang anticipated the next day's schedule. “Assuming the appointment is posted early, I'll immediately go to thank the treasurer, then to the governor...” “No.” Hu interrupted and waved his hand. “See the governor in the afternoon. When you return from the treasury, there's something important to do at the bureau. Gather the staff and let them know you're retaining the directorship. Why? To settle their minds. In banking, when a manager changes, the employees begin talking outside, or answer questions they cannot avoid. Many internal secrets escape that way. I imagine official life is the same. Once people feel secure, there'll be no rumours and needless trouble. Don't you agree?” “Of course!” Wang smiled. “My mind is quick enough, but always one step behind yours. We'll do that and discuss the rest at noon.”

After ten the following morning, the bureau's general affairs officer brought a draft drawn on Xinhe. Hu immediately went to Liu Qingsheng. His reasoning was this: Liu had promise, but his sudden promotion from counter clerk to manager might provoke disdain among fellow bankers. His standing and reputation must be developed. Handling the governor's remittance would demonstrate powerful connections. Within the province, the governor was the foremost possible client. With such a customer, everyone would view Liu differently. Once Hu explained, Liu was delighted—but not merely for himself. “What an unexpectedly splendid opportunity!” Then he grew serious. “Mr Hu, there's something I can tell you now. Mr Sun at Dayuan still doubts your backing and resources. It annoyed me, but I couldn't refute him. Empty words were useless, so I said nothing. If I arrange this remittance through Dayuan, they'll see your influence for themselves.” “So that's how it is?” Hu smiled. “Wait until our signboard is up. I'll show them a little more.” “Then I mustn't delay. I'll do it now and bring the documents to your house afterwards.”

Liu's standing had changed. He put on a silk robe and jacket bought at a second-hand clothing shop on Yanda Street, added new shoes and socks, and hired a small chair to Dayuan. The employees all looked up, expecting an important customer. When the curtain lifted and revealed Liu, they were astonished, envious, and admiring. He felt a little awkward, but his naturally smiling face made them reluctant to mock him. After a few civilities with Sun, he came to business. “I have a remittance to send to the capital through Dayuan. Send it to Rishengchang. That remittance house deals with the Board of Revenue, which will make things convenient.” “How much? Money to purchase office?” “No. Governor Huang's contribution to military funds: ten thousand taels of standard silver.” Sun's expression changed at once. “Why, Qingsheng!” He was surprised and impressed. “You've done well indeed, reaching the governor's circle.” “I have no such ability. Someone else entrusted it to me.” “Who?” Liu merely smiled, deliberately leaving him to guess. He knew the answer would be immediate but wanted the satisfaction of hearing Sun say it. “Hu Xueyan?” “Yes.” Liu looked at him and slowly nodded, as though asking whether he understood Hu now.

Puzzled and envious, Sun took the draft to the counter for processing, then returned. “Have you settled on a name for your firm?” “Yes. Fukang.” “Fukang!” Sun leaned closer and asked mysteriously, “Does Governor Huang have a share in it?” The notion surprised Liu. It was a serious suggestion. Repeated outside, it could become a boast of official backing and cause trouble. He answered immediately, “I don't know, but I shouldn't think so. How could a provincial governor open a bank in his own province?” “Of course you wouldn't know the inside story...” Sun smiled knowingly and said no more, wearing the reserved expression of a man possessing a private secret. Liu really did not know whether the governor held shares and could not deny it on anyone's behalf. He nevertheless felt uneasy. Once the remittance draft was ready, he took a chair to Hu's house, delivered it, and honestly reported Sun's speculation. Hu smiled with satisfaction. “Let them guess. The more excitement in the market, the easier Fukang's business will be.”

Reassured, Liu departed happily. Hu went to the bureau, where several chairs stood outside. Hangzhou's prefectural seat contained two counties, Qiantang and Renhe, with Qiantang the principal one. Its runners were clearing onlookers and managing traffic. Knowing that congratulatory visitors had arrived in numbers, Hu avoided the main entrance, slipped through a side door in the lane, and quietly entered his usual small room beside the private office. “Mr Hu!” Li Cheng, the office attendant, smiled as he delivered the news. “Our master has been promoted.” “Oh? To what?” “Wucheng County, with acting charge of Huzhou Prefecture, while retaining his bureau duties. Our master's official fortune is flourishing, and we servants benefit too. Mr Hu, I have a favour to ask.” “Go on.” “I have an uncle who's very good with his pen. A lawsuit ruined him, and he's in miserable circumstances. Could you put in a word and have him taken to Huzhou?” “Good with his pen in what way?” “People praise his social letters. He can also use an abacus and keep accounts.” Hu considered. “I'd like to try him first. Ask him to come and see me.” “Yes!” Li was excited. “When will you be free?”

Before Hu could answer, footsteps sounded and Wang's figure appeared outside the window. Li hurried to lift the curtain. Instead of entering his office, Wang came directly into Hu's small room. His face was radiant, his pace composed, and his bearing seemed altogether altered. “Congratulations!” Hu rose with a smile and bowed. “To both of us!” Wang took his hand. “Come and talk in my room.” He led Hu into the inner room of his office, and they sat side by side on the small bed where he took his afternoon rest. His excitement was irrepressible. “Xueyan, I couldn't believe it until I saw the treasurer this morning. Less than a year! Who could have imagined my position today? Misfortune lurks beside good fortune. I'm almost uneasy.” “You must remain steady. Today's result comes from yesterday's causes. Don't dwell on the past; look ahead. Never mind your present standing. Think only of what you've done today and what you ought to do.”

Taking his advice, Wang restrained himself and grew calmer. “First, there's something to discuss. The treasurer wants me to take office quickly. Someone else suggests accepting the seal on the first day of the fifth month, so I can collect the festival gifts already due. What do you think?” This baffled Hu. After careful thought, he answered, “I don't know official customs, but human feelings are the same. Before taking a ready-made benefit, consider whether it harms anyone. If it doesn't, well and good. Otherwise you're taking someone else's advantage. Put yourself in his place.” “That's exactly why I hesitate. There's only one set of festival gifts. If I take them, the present acting magistrate loses them...” “Then you absolutely mustn't!” Hu interrupted. “He's held the post for some time and deserves this payment. You shouldn't take it away. Money can be spent, but offending someone isn't easily repaired...” “Enough,” Wang interrupted in turn. “I've decided to receive the seal after the Dragon Boat Festival.” “Exactly. Your fortune is rising. You must handle things handsomely.” As he spoke, Hu handed over the remittance draft.

“This is important. I'll go to the governor after lunch. But even if I send in my card, he may have no time to see me.” Wang was earnest. “This must be settled promptly.” “He needn't necessarily see you. Enough heat will cook the pig's head: he only needs to see the draft. Write a letter beforehand and send that in if you can't get an audience. While you're there, distribute the customary festival gifts in his office early. Then you can rest easy; someone will bring news.” “Yes, that's what I'll do.” Wang paused. “Xueyan, taking up a regular post will mean advancing another ten thousand taels or so. The hole grows bigger and bigger. I'm worried.” “Don't be. You have me. Don't delay—go before the governor takes his nap.”

Wang followed the advice. He wrote a short letter, enclosed the draft, and prepared the festival gratuities, each in a red envelope. With a thick stack tucked inside his boot flap, he called for his chair and went to the governor's yamen. Liu Er hurried over with congratulations. Wang's standing had changed, and he could not resist assuming some importance. But while dignity showed on his face, a reward was ready in his hand. Once he passed over an envelope containing a twenty-tael note, the grander his manner, the more respectful Liu became. “Your Honour,” Liu said with great determination, “do you want to see the governor today? If you do, I'll make certain of it.” “Why? Is he very busy?” “Indeed. Otherwise I wouldn't say so.” Liu lowered his voice. “Someone has come from the capital. They've been behind closed doors in the private office all morning. The garrison general has also sent an orderly asking him over to discuss military affairs. Once he goes, he may not return until evening. If you must see him, I'll announce you now and contrive something. But even if you get in, there won't be much time.” “Before he visits the general, would he have time to read a letter?” “Certainly. Give it to me. I'll stay beside him and make sure he opens it.” Wang handed it over. “Then I rely on you. If the governor has any message, please come and let me know.” “Naturally. I understand.”

“One more favour.” Wang drew the handful of red envelopes from his boot and gave them to Liu. “A few small festival tokens. Please distribute them for me.” This was a duty Liu welcomed. With repeated assurances, he escorted Wang to his chair. Back at the bureau, the entrance was busier than ever, crowded with strangers. They rose respectfully at the sight of his chair. Sitting upright behind his dark spectacles, Wang examined them. Most were plainly seeking employment. He feared there were too many monks for too little porridge: he could not satisfy them all and would inevitably offend some. Sure enough, as soon as he sat down, a great bundle of cards and letters came in. Here was one of the hardships of office. Everyone had to be answered. Depending upon the importance of the connection, he received them personally or asked Zhou and others to do so. He had to devise countless polite phrases explaining what he could not do. Only when the sun touched the hills did the business briefly subside. Then he remembered Liu Er. Why had no message arrived? By lamplight there was still none, and Wang grew restless. Following Hu's advice, he had announced that morning, after returning from the treasury, that he would retain the bureau's directorship. He had hoped to steady the staff. If things changed and the pretence were exposed, the story would become a joke at his expense. He could not bear that loss of face. As he worried, Hu arrived. Hearing the situation, he too found it puzzling, but retained his confidence. There was no good news, but no bad news either. There was no need for alarm.

“Even so, Liu should have told me something.” “He doesn't know why you're waiting. If he understood your anxiety, he'd certainly have come.” Hu thought a moment. “Go home first, and send Gao to invite him over. We can ask how the governor responded.” “That makes sense.” Gao too was gone a long time without word. Wang and Hu drank together at home while they waited. Not until the clock struck nine did Gao appear with a lantern, lighting Liu's way inside. Now that the man had arrived, Wang became composed and first asked whether he had eaten. Liu had eaten long before. “When Second Master Gao came, I was still reporting upstairs. There were many instructions, which delayed me. The governor read your letter early, but only now gave me a message.” “Oh?” Liu's unhurried manner made Wang impatient, though he would not show it. “His Excellency says: after His Honour Wang has received the seal at Huzhou and put things in order, he is to return promptly to the provincial capital. The business here is important too.” “Here” naturally meant the Sea Transport Bureau. Wang was overwhelmed with joy. He and Hu exchanged a smile that needed no words.

Only then did Liu understand. Wang's retention of the bureau had not been certain until this moment. He regretted his ignorance. Had he known, this news could have been made a valuable commodity, with a more elaborate account of his own services. But it was not too late. He immediately bent his knees in salute. “Congratulations, Your Honour! Knowing how anxiously you awaited news, I stayed beside our master without daring to move. At last I obtained the good word.” “I am most grateful.” Wang understood and sent him away with another envelope containing ten taels.

“At last you've got what you wished, and everyone can be satisfied.” Hu joked, “Your Honour Wang, I have an assignment to request. Let me hire the boat for your journey to take office.” Naturally, this meant giving A'zhu's family the business. Wang laughed too. “Any other assignment is yours. Only that one is out of the question.” Their laughter drew Mrs Wang out to inquire. That was her excuse; she really wanted to hear the news and share the joy of her husband's rising fortune. They had become intimate family friends, so she no longer avoided Hu. Sitting with them, she thanked him repeatedly, then asked, “Young Master Hu, why don't you purchase an official title?” “Exactly!” Wang seized on it. “This is important. A qualification would make your work much easier. At the bureau, for instance, if you held a department or county magistrate's qualification, I could recommend you as a commissioner to oversee everything for me. Wouldn't that simplify matters?” “True. But my first concern is getting Fukang established.” Hu glanced at Mrs Wang. Understanding that some things could not be said before her, Wang found an excuse to send her away. “Fukang must open soon,” Hu continued. “We need those tens of thousands from the treasury as capital. Press them again tomorrow. I've already found someone to work on the matter below.” “That can be done. My mind is in such confusion that I don't know what to do first.” “I don't fully understand official practice. Let's discuss it patiently. We have the whole night to put things in order.” They talked through the night, writing down each task and its priority. Hu busied himself preparing Fukang. Wang's first major duty was to find private secretaries.

Private secretaries came in many varieties. Besides the legal and revenue advisers, there were accountants handling receipts and payments, correspondence secretaries, tutors for the official's children, examination assistants who read papers, collection specialists, and others. The legal and revenue posts were naturally the most important. Secretary Yu at the judicial commissioner's yamen had long promised to find suitable men, so Wang made a special call. His purpose needed no explanation. Yu had already chosen his own pupil for the legal post. This pupil, Qin Shoumen, was in fact nearly Yu's age and no novice. The profession was sometimes dismissed as a last resort for men who failed in their studies, but a secretary's life could be that of “an immortal, a tiger, or a dog.” Celebrated secretaries enjoyed great prestige. They needed not only command of statutes and precedents and a fluent pen, but sound professional lineage, broad knowledge, and experience. Their training was therefore crucial. Qin had followed Yu for years, beginning at county and department level, progressing through prefectural and circuit offices, and finally reaching the provincial judicial commission. He understood the entire local judicial process and the powers and characteristics of every level. This comprehensive experience made him superior to men trained only in a county office or only at the provincial commission. He had begun independent practice ten years earlier and had never lacked employment. Two years before, both parents died. He returned to Shaoxing for their funerals, then fell ill himself. Recently recovered, he had come to his teacher for assistance. Yu could now recommend him to Wang. They met and conversed agreeably. Wang reflected that, besides ability, secretaries needed connections and channels of communication; otherwise even great talent achieved little for the effort. Since Yu had introduced Qin, he would naturally support cases submitted from the county to the province. One salary would effectively secure two advisers. An excellent bargain.

They immediately agreed upon the engagement, to mutual satisfaction. Wang used the same method for the revenue post, asking the most celebrated Secretary Wang in the treasury to recommend someone. He proposed a fellow pupil, Yang Yongzhi, stating plainly that the man was diligent and honest rather than exceptionally able. That suited Wang, who chiefly wanted the connection with Secretary Wang. He himself knew much of revenue administration, so a less capable adviser would not matter. Back at the bureau, he personally prepared the letters of engagement on large red cards. The front bore the words “Letter of Engagement.” Inside Qin's, he wrote: “I respectfully engage Master Qin Shoumen to manage legal affairs during my tenure as acting magistrate of Wucheng County and acting prefect of Huzhou, at a monthly remuneration of seventy taels of standard silver, commencing upon arrival. A further ceremonial gift of eight taels will be offered at each of the three major festivals. This engagement is hereby confirmed.” He signed himself humbly as Wang Youling, bowing his head. Neither official nor private seal was used. The card went into a red envelope labelled “For Master Qin's keeping.” Yang's letter followed the same form, but offered fifty taels a month and expressly excluded additional festival gifts, since a revenue secretary received other benefits after each collection of land and grain taxes.

After sending the letters, Wang issued dinner invitations. Though they held no official rank, private secretaries enjoyed standing equal to that of their employer. The legal and revenue advisers in particular had a prescribed form of address: since a local magistrate was called “His Honour,” they were accorded the corresponding honour as secretarial masters. They were invited separately. Secretaries insisted upon ceremony, maintaining a domain of their own within the yamen. An official seeking advice went to them. On the first and fifteenth of each month he dressed formally to pay his respects, much as at an official audience. Special banquets were offered on festivals. At ordinary dinners a secretary must occupy the seat of honour or not be invited at all. Although the two had not yet joined him, Wang must already follow the rules. To avoid deciding which should sit first and which second, he entertained them separately, giving each the first seat. Hu, Zhou, and Wu would accompany him. Qin was invited first, but declined by letter because he observed a strict vegetarian diet and did not wish to cause trouble. This was easily remedied. The vegetarian food of Hangzhou's four great monasteries was exquisite. At Jingci Monastery beneath Leifeng Pagoda, the abbot Xinwu was Wang's fellow townsman and an old acquaintance. Wang sent a new invitation promising a carefully prepared vegetarian meal, which Qin gladly accepted. On the appointed day, their chairs left through Qingbo Gate. They boarded a boat at “Listening to Orioles among the Willows,” toured West Lake, and then ate. Abbot Xinwu joined them as half host, half guest. Asked why he had become a lifelong vegetarian, Qin answered frankly.

“With the abbot present, I dare not speak falsely. I am repenting past wrongdoing. A few years ago, while employed at the Shuntian prefectural yamen, I mistakenly trusted someone's account and allowed a guilty man to escape his proper punishment. Although I bore no formal responsibility, my conscience remained troubled. Soon afterwards both my parents died. I resigned, returned home, and arranged their funerals, then fell dangerously ill myself. During the illness I repented and vowed that, if I survived, I would henceforth abstain from meat and recite Buddhist prayers. The bodhisattva evidently took pity on my sincerity. I improved day by day. Now I am fulfilling that vow.” “Sincerity brings a response,” Xinwu said, nodding repeatedly. “Plant melons and you reap melons; plant beans and you reap beans. Cause and consequence cannot be disregarded.” “I intended to lay down my pen altogether, but my family obligations are heavy, and I have had to return to the profession. It is easy to do wrong in public office. I have nothing with which to repay my employer's kindness except to cultivate some merit on his behalf.” “Indeed,” Wang answered earnestly. “That is exactly what I hope for.” “One can also cultivate virtue in public service,” Hu reassured him. “You must have done much good without realising it.” “Naturally, there has been some. Our professional rule, passed from master to pupil for years, is ‘Save the living, not the dead,’ in accordance with Heaven's love of life. Though, frankly, there are rewards in that too.” The words were discreet, but everyone understood. Saving the living brought monetary gifts. If one merely sought justice for the dead, who but the bereaved would show gratitude? “Still, our profession does more good than harm. It differs from prison officials and jailers, for whom wrongdoing is easy and merit difficult.”

“Why is that?” Hu asked with interest. “Simply because we can ultimately decide for ourselves. An employer like Mr Xuexuan would naturally forbid wrongdoing. Even under the wrong man, if we hold firm, he cannot force us against our principles. Prison is different. There truly is no daylight there.” “How so?” “In a word, nothing happens without money. Without it, the place is worse than a pigsty. With it, one lives as comfortably as at home. Food and lodging are excellent, and even wives or concubines can come in to spend the night.” “I've heard that too,” Wang said. “Does it really happen?” “Certainly. Let me tell you a story to accompany your wine. It happened here in Zhejiang, during the Daoguang reign.”

A young man from a rich family had committed a serious homicide. County, prefectural, circuit, and provincial authorities all upheld immediate execution by beheading. Only the Board of Punishments' authorisation remained before the sentence could be carried out. He was the family's sole male heir for three generations. They spent money on every possible approach in the hope of saving him. But the facts were clear and the officials honest. Their considerable expenditure benefited only the intermediaries. His father could not bear to see the line end and his enormous fortune eventually divided among distant clansmen beyond the prescribed degrees of mourning. On someone's advice, he took a substantial gift to a legal secretary renowned for ingenious schemes, nicknamed “the Man Even Ghosts Fear.” Unable to save his son, he asked for the next best thing: could the prisoner leave a child, even a girl? There was a method, though naturally nobody could guarantee a son. The secretary promised three more months of life. During that time, several healthy women considered likely to bear sons would be paid generously to visit the prisoner. The jailers had already been bribed, so access was unrestricted. Each dawn someone would meet the women at the back gate and take them to the wealthy household, where they were maintained. It was agreed beforehand that they would stay several months. Those who did not conceive would receive money and leave; those who did would remain until the birth, with further arrangements made afterwards.

Yet after only a dozen days, the ministry's reply arrived in a cord-fastened sealed dispatch. One glance showed that it authorised immediate execution. “Wait!” Hu interrupted. “Didn't you say he had three months? It hasn't even been one.” “Be patient.” Qin smiled. “There is naturally another explanation. Otherwise, why would even ghosts fear the man?” He continued the story.

An immediate-execution order required the execution party to be assembled as soon as the sealed dispatch arrived. The magistrate took his seat, summoned the yamen personnel and executioner, and had the prisoner brought from jail. He opened the dispatch in court—and froze. The name on the cover was correct, but everything inside was wrong: the name, the case, the place. A document meant for Guizhou had reached Zhejiang. Without proper authorisation, how could he execute the man? The prisoner returned to jail and the document was sent back. Even a slow journey from Hangzhou to the capital took no more than twenty days, but the ministry had to wait for Guizhou to return the other misdirected document. Yunnan and Guizhou seemed half a world away. The round trip would take more than three months. The prisoner there benefited too, unexpectedly gaining several months of life. “Naturally, someone at the ministry had arranged it?” Wang asked. “Yes. A secretary at the Board of Punishments was persuaded. It counted as negligence, punishable by three months' salary—only a few dozen taels. But this effortless act of ‘negligence’ cost a thousand taels to arrange.” “A good deed!” Hu laughed. “To preserve a family line is great hidden merit, and brings a thousand taels besides. Why not do it?”

“But what of the damage to the law?” Qin asked. “If orders for sealing property or confiscating an estate suffered similar complications, who would compensate the treasury?” “Would that count as negligence too?” “Such important matters admit no negligence, nor would it occur by accident. Law cannot be separated from human motives. When hearing cases and enforcing it, examine those motives and the doubts become apparent. Suppose a habitually meticulous man suddenly makes a mistake, and the mistake makes an enormous difference. That is suspicious. Or take a class of cases always decided one way. Suddenly the responsible official declares that practice unjust, rejects it, or even overturns a final judgement. If this case was unjust, were the earlier identical cases not unjust too? Why not reverse them? Consider that carefully, and the hidden interference becomes obvious.” These remarks showed Qin's clear understanding of affairs. Wang was naturally pleased.

But legal affairs mattered enormously to a magistrate's career. They were also the first basis upon which the people judged their parent-official. With good harvests and a prosperous district, they might tolerate somewhat excessive additions to taxes and miscellaneous levies. If the rightful party lost a lawsuit and the wrongdoer won, however, even an innocent mistake would provoke deep resentment and accusations of corruption and injustice. Wang therefore valued Qin more highly than Yang. He had agreed with Hu beforehand that, since he could not repeatedly question his new adviser himself, Hu should test him through conversation. He now gave another signal. Hu adopted an expression of partial understanding and asked with curious admiration, “Everyone says a legal master's pen is formidable: one altered character can determine a family's fortune. They also say the finest writing comes from secretaries' offices. I've asked about it without receiving a clear explanation. Today you can surely enlighten me.” This double compliment, to his profession and himself, pleased Qin. Half warmed by wine and enjoying the discussion, he smiled with restrained pride. “‘Read ten thousand volumes but neglect the law—how will you guide your sovereign to the virtue of Yao and Shun?’ The claim about writing refers to its practical use. As for a single character determining a family's fortune, that is true. But manipulating words is our profession's great taboo. In short: where no trouble exists, don't create it; where trouble arises, don't fear it.” Everyone nodded. Wu, who had some literary education, particularly admired the warning against manipulating words and asked for an explanation. “First, not creating trouble where none exists...” Qin began.

He gave an example. A governor disliked his provincial treasurer and wanted him removed. Unfortunately, the treasurer was both honest and capable, leaving no fault to seize upon. At last an opportunity came. During a sacrifice at the Confucian temple, the treasurer had a severe cold and coughed continually through the ceremony. The governor discussed this lapse with his secretary. Obeying his employer's wishes, the secretary used elaborate wording to make a great affair of it, impeaching the treasurer for ceremonial misconduct and disrespect. The court usually investigated before acting upon an accusation. Grave cases brought a special commissioner from the capital by express relay. Matters of this kind were often referred to the garrison general or provincial education commissioner. That province had no resident garrison general, but every province had an education commissioner. He too had attended the sacrifice and knew that the treasurer's conduct was involuntary. Even if it amounted to a breach of decorum, a reprimand afterwards should have sufficed. Why magnify a trifle into a special memorial of impeachment? Resenting this, he wanted not only to help the treasurer but to make the governor suffer. Yet an open criticism might lead the court to suspect partiality, making the wording difficult. Before passing the provincial and metropolitan examinations, the education commissioner had trained in legal work. After much thought, he found inspiration in the governor's claim to have “personally witnessed” the offence. His reply said that, although present, he could not verify it: “My place was in the forward rank; propriety forbade looking behind.” Those unobtrusive words made the matter plain to the Grand Councillors. The governor too had knelt ahead of the treasurer. How could he have seen misconduct behind him? He must himself have broken decorum by turning round. Both officials were punished. With plaintiff and defendant treated alike, the plaintiff lost face, while the defendant, though punished, felt satisfied.

“Truly, there was no trouble until a foolish man made it,” Wu said. “The fault lay in the governor's secretary failing to remonstrate firmly.” “You've identified the essential point.” Qin glanced at Wang. “Once an employer has honoured us with his trust, we must hold to unshakable principles. Compliance for a moment that leaves trouble for the future harms both him and us. It must never happen. Unfortunately, loyal advice often jars upon the ear, and few employers have no temper.” “Rest assured,” Wang promptly declared. “Having entrusted the post to you, I shall naturally leave legal affairs to your judgement.” “With that assurance, I can act confidently. Taking advantage of this hospitality, let me apologise in advance and ask you to forgive any future appearance of overstepping my authority.” He raised his cup. Wang gladly accepted the toast. Host and guest were perfectly at ease, and everyone shared their pleasure. After a noisy round of drinking, they returned to the interrupted subject.

“Now for not fearing trouble when it comes,” Wu said loudly. “Please give us an example of that too.” Qin considered briefly. “It means keeping one's composure. A steady temper settles the mind; a settled mind allows clear thought. Then an apparently lost position may yield an inspired move. However detailed the law, ancient or modern, there are always gaps. Reasoning is similar. Sometimes an argument is unsound, but familiarity keeps everyone from noticing. Something apparently inconceivable may, on examination, prove entirely reasonable and beyond refutation. With composure, breadth, and depth of thought, one can find the opening, avoid the heavier consequence, and turn a great problem into a small one, then into none. Since we mentioned cord-fastened dispatches, let me tell you an ingenious story about one. I suppose my employer has seen them?” “Yes,” Wang replied. “Originally their fastening signified confidentiality. They were used not only for execution orders but for arresting important criminals. In time the practice became a formality: a flap fixed to the cover, tied with thin hemp cord. Anyone could open it. The most confidential document became the least secure—an outcome surely never intended.” “Exactly. This story turns upon that freedom to open them. Such dispatches travelled by post relay. Each county through which they passed added its official seal. An inquisitive magistrate handling one might open it, read it, and tie it up again. One such magistrate was a heavy opium smoker. Every evening he read official papers while reclining beside his pipe. One night, half dazed, he opened a dispatch and accidentally burned its contents over the opium lamp.”

That brought him sharply to his senses. Destroying a confidential dispatch was an appalling offence. He hurried to seek his legal secretary's help. “Do you still have the cover?” “Yes.” “Then don't worry. Give it to me, and bring the official seal.” The magistrate obeyed. The secretary folded a blank sheet, put it inside, tied the cord, stamped the seal, and handed it back. “Send it by relay to the next station.” “Will that do?” the magistrate asked hesitantly. “What if the next station discovers it?” “Think for yourself. Suppose you're the next magistrate. You open it and find a blank sheet. What would you do?” Qin needed to go no further. Everyone understood. Anyone finding the blank page would dare neither announce the discovery nor return it and cause trouble: that would first expose his own offence of opening a confidential document. The reasoning resembled the education commissioner's statement that his forward position forbade looking behind.

“Though legal advisers belong to the school of law, they should also read Laozi and Zhuangzi to gain such insights,” Wang reflected. “A man must not allow his vision to be obstructed, seeing an autumn hair but missing a cartload of firewood. There are so many obvious truths that people nevertheless fail to see. How can one explain it?” The discussion moved to other matters. They talked until sunset, then left the table and rowed back to the city. The following day, Wang entertained the revenue secretary Yang Yongzhi aboard a pleasure boat on West Lake, again accompanied by Hu, Zhou, and Wu. Fukang was expected to use Huzhou Prefecture's and Wucheng County's public remittances to the provincial treasury as capital. Since the revenue secretary was closely involved, Hu made a special effort to cultivate him. Yang was straightforward and honest, and therefore easy to manage. Hu soon made him wholly accommodating, with the feeling that they should have met long before. In fact, the method was simple. Straightforward men liked to be consulted and generally shared all they knew. Hu spoke well, but listened still better. However dull another man's words, he could attend gravely, eyes fixed upon him, as though fascinated. He really did listen, adding a remark or developing a point at the crucial moment. The speaker then felt deeply understood, and congenial conversation became close friendship.

Yang was not exceptionally able, but his agreeable temperament had given him many acquaintances. Hu's company drew him into an animated account of contemporary figures. Eventually, discussing Huzhou, he mentioned Qian Jiang and asked whether Wang knew him. “I've heard of him. He comes from Changxing County in Huzhou Prefecture. He became known through being exiled to Ili with our Fujian statesman Lin Wenzhong. They say he's an extraordinary man. Someone appreciated by Lord Lin can't be ordinary. Why do you mention him? Is there news?” “You could call it news. But it affects local officials profoundly, and we don't yet know the court's view.” “Please explain.” “We must begin with a senior official. You know Lei Yixian?” “Yes. A Hubei man. As senior vice censor-in-chief, he joined the Director-General of River Conservancy to inspect the Yellow River's outlet. Recently I read that he volunteered to fight the rebels. He has recruited ten thousand men, stationed them at Gaoyou north of the Yangtze, and is guarding the southeastern approach to Yangzhou. He's won several battles.” “Exactly. Qian Jiang serves on his staff. Troops without pay cannot fight. The court's position is that anyone able to recruit men and raise funds should devise his own means, and it will approve. I hear Qian has proposed collection offices and checkpoints at important land and water routes. Travelling merchants are assessed on the value of their goods, generally one part in a thousand. The levy is called lijin. Local shops pay on the same basis. The receipts are considerable, and other provinces are reportedly considering imitation. But since it harms trade, the court may refuse it.”

This news, and Yang's view that the proposed lijin would harm merchants, gave Wang his opportunity. He and Hu had discussed the two secretaries carefully. Law was outside Wang's expertise, so he must rely upon Qin and first test his ability. Revenue administration was different: Wang understood it well. Yet secretaries traditionally worked independently and disliked interference. An accommodating one might give an outwardly polite response; an autocratic one would simply ignore his employer. Hu's plan was therefore to win Yang's affection while Wang demonstrated enough knowledge to command respect. With gratitude and apprehension working together, Yang could be brought under effective direction. Wang seized the moment to display his learning. “I'm not sure it necessarily harms trade,” he began in an argumentative tone. “Our dynasty's tax system differs from those of earlier times. Whenever war comes, military funds must be raised separately. Comparatively speaking, lijin may still offer more benefit than harm.” This broad proposition served as the introduction to an essay. Intent upon demonstrating his knowledge, Wang began at the beginning. From ancient times, the chief annual revenues had been land and poll taxes and grain levies. Repeated additional assessments late in the Ming had made life intolerable. Farmers suffered so greatly that they abandoned their fields and fled. This was a major cause of the spread of roaming rebels and, ultimately, the dynasty's fall.

After the Qing entered China, the Kangxi emperor's suppression of the Three Feudatories finally secured the dynasty's foundations. Taking warning from the Ming, he issued an edict promising never to increase taxation. This was one of the dynasty's great benevolent measures and a principal reason the Manchus could long rule the central plains. Later emperors faithfully maintained it. Customs and salt duties also supplied annual revenue, but land and poll taxes represented two-thirds of the total. With an undertaking never to increase them, annual receipts were effectively fixed. They could cover expenditure in peaceful years of favourable weather. But war brought extra military costs with no provision. Drought or flood required both tax remissions and famine relief: income fell while expenditure rose. How could that be managed? If war and natural disaster coincided, both sides of the crisis intensified.

“There are two ways to meet the shortfall,” Wang continued calmly. “The first is savings accumulated in ordinary times. Though the emperor possesses all within the four seas, state revenue and palace revenue are separate. The distinction was already well developed under the Han: the Grand Minister of Agriculture managed public expenditure, while the Privy Treasurer managed the sovereign's private wealth. If the ruler has a surplus while the state lacks funds, disorder follows. When the founding Song emperor subdued the Ten Kingdoms, their gold, silver, and jewels went into the palace treasury, but were separately sealed as a special reserve. He intended to accumulate enough to buy back the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun. Unfortunately, the unworthy Huizong spent the palace reserves on the Genyue pleasure garden, after which the Jin invaded. The Ming needs no elaboration: its Board of Revenue was desperately poor while palace wealth piled high, only to fall into the rebels' hands. Our dynasty is different. Reserves are held in the state treasury, not the Imperial Household Department.”

Wang then cited treasury balances: fifty million taels in Kangxi's forty-eighth year, falling to eight million by the end; after thirteen years of vigorous reform under Yongzheng, an unprecedented sixty million at Qianlong's accession; and seventy million in Qianlong's forty-sixth year. After Jiaqing, however, the position deteriorated, worsening further under Daoguang. “When the late emperor died, the Board held eight million taels. I don't know the figures for the last three years. Since Hong and Yang rose, money has flowed like water. I imagine the dynasty has never been poorer.”

The mixture of narrative and analysis enlightened not only Zhou and Wu but Yang himself. Revenue was his profession, yet he knew only local finance and little of the central treasury. Hearing Wang explain it so coherently, he thought that, purchased qualification or not, his employer had considerable learning. At that very moment Wang turned to purchased office. “The second way to meet a public shortfall is through contributions paid for official qualifications. The system began under the Han, when money could obtain a position as a palace gentleman. Later dynasties retained it, but none used it as extensively as ours.” He described its development and connection with central revenue. Contributions for actual appointments had begun under Kangxi to fund the war against the Three Feudatories. By Yongzheng's reign they had become a regular practice, their proceeds effectively part of annual revenue, though at a relatively modest average of around fifteen per cent. Excessive use began under Jiaqing. The proceeds often equalled half the year's revenue, and in his seventh year exceeded eighty per cent. “Once the system is abused, its evils are beyond description,” Wang said evenly. “Though I myself entered by purchase, I can hardly respect that class of official. Anyone with money, however ignorant, can obtain office. Having first invested capital, he treats administration like a business. Once appointed, he must recover principal and interest. How can clean government result?”

“That cannot be said of everyone,” Wu objected. “Advancement by examination is naturally the proper path. But examination success doesn't depend on writing alone. Fate, luck, and favourable circumstances play their part, leaving many capable men unrecognised. Purchase opens a door through which they can exercise their talents instead of being buried. That too is a great service.” The compliment to Wang was implicit and understood. He saw no need to disclaim it. “Cases like mine are uncommon. Even one advantage cannot compensate for a hundred harms. Now military expenses are widening an already overused system until the streets are full of officials. What sense does that make?” “Your view is entirely sound,” Yang answered, sincerely convinced. Without noticing his reversal, he changed his argument. “Commercial taxes in our dynasty are not heavy. Apart from such miscellaneous charges as brokers' licence fees, pawnshop duties, and livestock taxes, ordinary trade pays only the tax on goods brought from elsewhere for sale in local shops—the landing tax, also called the stationary tax. Goods in transit pay only customs duties. A moderate additional lijin levy would not be excessive.” “Precisely!” Wang said, already wondering privately whether Zhejiang too might introduce it.

The discussion had achieved its purpose. Hu changed the subject. Impressed by Qian Jiang, he asked whether Yang knew him. “Not only do I know him; we're distantly related. His courtesy names are Qiuping and Dongping. An ancestor was governor of Shandong, and his father also served there. He was exceptional from childhood, quick at everything except that he disliked eight-legged essays.” “How else would he be an extraordinary man?” Wu laughed. “Someone like that must disregard conventional restraints and have ambitions of his own.” “He proposed another measure now being adopted across the provinces.” Yang suddenly looked at Hu. “You could make use of it yourself.” “What measure?” “Another of Qian Dongping's ideas: obtain imperial permission to draw blank qualification certificates in advance and issue them as soon as contributions are paid. Everyone finds it convenient, so ‘business’ is excellent. This province has begun doing the same. You could purchase a qualification.”

That appealed to Hu. His recent experience in official circles had taught him the importance of standing, not for display but for convenience. When making or receiving calls and exchanging names, a recognised qualification settled the proper forms of address without awkwardness. As an untitled commoner, he felt out of place everywhere. Friends could address one another as brothers, but with unfamiliar officials he risked either diminishing himself or offending them. It was a serious difficulty. That evening he specially consulted Wang, who naturally approved. “I've urged you to do it for ages! I don't know why you've kept delaying.” “No time. The business is troublesome. Apart from the time it takes, there are objections and demands for fees at every stage, enough to destroy anyone's enthusiasm. Immediate issue, with money handed over and the certificate received in return, is different.” “There will still be demands. ‘Immediate’ won't be quite so immediate. But avoiding collection from the ministry itself will certainly make it much faster.”

“That shows how necessary it is to think. In finance, opportunities are everywhere.” Hu drew another lesson. “Whether an official dealing with the people or a merchant dealing with customers, if you want the money in their purses, make them comfortable enough to open those purses willingly.” “There's truth in that.” Wang nodded thoughtfully. “At Huzhou, I too must find a way to ‘serve’ the people comfortably, so they'll gladly pay their taxes.” “They're easy enough to serve. Avoid official bluster and deal with realities; they'll call you a good official.” Hu returned to his own business. “What qualification should I purchase?” “Department or county magistrate,” Wang answered without hesitation. “Entrust it to Yang Yongzhi.” Taking his advice, Hu sent Yang a formal invitation the next day and entertained him at a restaurant.

After three rounds of wine, they discussed the matter. Yang readily agreed and made an announcement. “Beyond the prescribed contribution, there are always miscellaneous charges from which everyone handling the business receives a benefit. I'll deduct my own share and reduce the miscellaneous fees by thirty per cent.” “That won't do. A gentleman may love money, provided he acquires it properly. Whatever is due to you should be accepted without hesitation.” “Would that be friendship?” Yang waved his hand. “Leave that to me. What I need to know is whether you want the basic qualification or additional preferences.” There were many variations in purchasing office. The simplest was an empty title supported by a ministry certificate, conferring standing, family distinction, and local prestige. An actual appointment required choices concerning priority and the province in which one would serve. Hu had other powerful support and no wish to travel to the capital, register with the Board of Civil Office, and await selection. He merely wanted the title “His Honour Hu” while continuing to run his bank. Additional expenditure was unnecessary. “I only need the ministry certificate. Am I really going to be an official?” “It wouldn't be difficult, and you'd be a favourite of the first order. But each man has his ambitions. Bring the silver tomorrow. I'll pay it in and obtain the certificate as quickly as possible.”

Hu thanked him and said no more about the purchase. He diligently pressed wine upon Yang, strengthening their friendship while asking what opportunities existed around local revenue receipts and expenditure. Honest though Yang was, and warmly as he regarded Hu, he would not say much on those matters. Hu's quick understanding nevertheless enabled him to infer several methods from the hints he received. The next day, he took the purchase money from the five thousand taels set aside for opening the bank. The official contribution was made into a draft, the miscellaneous charges supplied in silver, and both delivered to Yang. True to his word, Yang returned the portion of the fees that would have been his own benefit.

By now it was the end of the fourth month. Wang was overwhelmed with preparations for taking office, and Hu was busier still, both advising him and establishing the bank. Fortunately, Liu was extremely capable. He had taken a handsome building in pledge at Yunsi Hexia and personally supervised its painting and plastering. Signboards, furniture, employees—he managed everything inside and out. Rising early and retiring late, he grew dark and thin with fatigue, but his delight in the opportunity made the work seem no hardship. An auspicious day had been chosen for Wang to take office: the ninth of the fifth month. Invitations to farewell dinners poured in. Doing business was easier than being an official; social obligations could not be neglected. Wang was distressed by the lack of time. When Zhang's invitation arrived, he hoped to evade it. “Look,” he said to Hu with a rueful smile, “Zhang has joined the crowd! Please explain for me. Let him keep his dinner until I return to the provincial capital.” Hu thought their relationship with Zhang too special, their interests too closely connected, for Wang to deny him this respect. Yet the invitations showed two or three engagements every day. After a moment he had an idea. “I had intended to offer a little hospitality myself...” “Between brothers, that can certainly be dispensed with,” Wang interrupted. “Let me finish. I'd thought of giving Zhang my place in the schedule. He's a good man, and we should accommodate him. Since there's no time, why not serve his banquet aboard the boat?” “I don't quite understand.”

“Zhang and I can accompany you for part of the journey. We'll have his farewell dinner aboard and return the next day.” “That's a good idea! In fact, Xueyan,” Wang smiled, “why return at all? Come all the way to Huzhou.” “Please understand my position. Once Fukang is in order, I'll come at once. You haven't taken office yet; we know nothing of the situation in Huzhou. Even if I wished to help, I couldn't begin. Besides, the bureau's affairs matter too.” “That reminds me!” Wang asked sharply, “When will your certificate arrive?” “Soon, I expect.” “Press Yang to finish it quickly. I've already spoken to Treasurer Lin. As soon as the certificate arrives, you'll be appointed a convoy commissioner at the bureau. Then you can manage everything for me.” “That isn't the best arrangement. Nominally, Zhou should act as executive director. He'll consult me on everything, so nothing will suffer. If I take his distinction, he'll develop private grievances and things may go badly.” Wang saw the reason and agreed. “In any case, the sooner the purchase is completed, the better.”

“Yes. It concerns more than this one matter. Once you've taken up your post, I'll establish myself properly too: move house, make a little display, and begin afresh.” “Excellent!” Wang smiled. “Then you'll be His Honour Hu of Fukang Bank.” Though teasing, he had expressed Hu's intention exactly. Hu was limiting his public activities until he had the qualification, the bank was open, and the necessary appearance established. Then he could present a wholly new face and make a striking entrance, enabling him to act freely and find support on every side.

Leaving the bureau, Hu went to Xinhe. Zhang had been about to go out, but changed his plans on seeing him. He had much to discuss and rarely managed to find Hu. Now that Hu had come of his own accord, he would not lightly surrender the opportunity for a long talk. “Xueyan, you're busier and richer every day. Getting a word with you is harder than seeing a great official.” Hu heard the wrong note and quickly explained. “Mr Zhang, I'm merely run off my feet. How could I put on airs with you? Send an apprentice to my house, and would I dare not come?” “You put it too strongly!” Zhang knew he had gone too far and hastened to repair the impression. “We're brothers. A joke or two shouldn't be taken seriously.” “Naturally not. But today I have come with a purpose...” Hu explained the proposed change to Wang's farewell dinner, and Zhang readily agreed. “I hear you've purchased a magistrate's qualification?” “Yes.” Before another question could follow, Hu gave the full history of the decision. If Zhang still felt any resentment, this openness dispelled it. “Xueyan,” he said with genuine pleasure, “you'll rise far. And since you began at Xinhe, I'll share the credit.”

Hu smiled without answering, then rose. “You were about to go out. I won't detain you. We'll talk another day.” “Oh!” Zhang suddenly said. “Old Zhang came by.” “Which Old Zhang?” “Look at you! You remember his daughter but not her father.” “Ah...” Hu smiled. “A'zhu's father.” “Exactly. I don't know how he found me. He'd just returned from Shanghai and heard that His Honour was appointed to Huzhou. He insisted that his boat be chosen for the journey. I said I knew nothing of the arrangements and he must ask you. I gave him your address.” “I can't help him either. A new official has people arranging his journey. If I interfere even in trifles like that, everyone will curse me.” “That's no concern of mine.” Zhang laughed. “He'll come to see you. If you're not afraid of A'zhu cursing you, refuse him.” “How about this?” Hu had a sudden idea. “We're accompanying Mr Xuexuan for a stage and returning the following day. We'll need a boat too. We can use Old Zhang's.” “Exactly. That gives you a satisfactory answer for A'zhu.”

Zhang's constant references to A'zhu revived Hu's feelings. Remembering her slight frowns and smiles, her changes from sorrow to happiness, he found much to dwell upon. The following morning he deliberately remained at home, drawing up a list of prospective customers for Fukang while waiting for Old Zhang so he could hire the boat. But it was the wife who came. A newly engaged maid, A'xiang, announced that “Mrs Zhang” wished to see him. At first Hu was puzzled; then he thought of A'zhu's mother. Looking through the glass window, he confirmed it. Mrs Zhang, then! She too came from a good family, and for A'zhu's sake he might raise her standing a little. He went out and greeted her accordingly. “You are too kind, Mr Hu.” She put down her gifts and curtsied. “I've long wanted to pay my respects to Mrs Hu, but we've been so busy making a living. Where is she?” A female caller should ordinarily be received in the rear hall. But his wife did not know the circumstances, and he wanted to explain first. He therefore diverted the conversation. “Inside. Why bring presents? You are too generous.” “Only some plain things I've made, probably not fit to eat. A small token.” She opened the paper packages and woven basket, releasing a rich aroma. There were her celebrated Wuxi pork ribs, smoked green beans, square cakes, and zongzi—snacks for which Huzhou was famous. “These I must accept. One can't buy their like outside. Wait a moment; I'll call my wife.” In the rear hall he explained the visitor's true identity, naturally omitting A'zhu. He said only that she was a daughter of a scholarly family and had come to seek business. But since she had called, she was a guest, and his wife should receive her.

The women exchanged greetings. Mrs Hu found the visitor congenial; the visitor inspected her hostess with particular care. Their intent scrutiny from head to foot made Hu uncomfortable. Soon their household conversation left him aside. With little time to spare, he had to interrupt. “Mrs Zhang, you're a little late. His Honour's boat to Huzhou has already been hired.” Now that business was being discussed, Mrs Hu need no longer remain. She offered the customary invitations to stay comfortably and take a simple meal, then withdrew. “You're fortunate, Mr Hu. Your wife is virtuous and looks good-tempered.” A'zhu's mother pressed the point. “She has a very good temper, doesn't she?” Hu was surprised by this irrelevant concern. “Quite good.” He nodded. “Would your boat take a short journey?” “Of course. Where?” “Only to Linping.” He explained the reason. “Nothing could be better. Tell Mr Zhang he needn't trouble to prepare the banquet. Use our cooking. His Honour must be tired of shark's fin and sea cucumber. I'll devise a few light, unusual dishes. The guests will be pleased, and the hosts will spend less.” “Don't worry about saving us money. Just make the food good.” “Yes. I understand.”

The business was settled, and she should have been able to leave contentedly. Yet she remained, apparently unable to bring up something else. Hu noticed but could not guess what she wanted. “Is there anything more?” Asked directly, she had to speak. First she carefully looked behind the screen, as though afraid of being overheard. Hu leaned forward with closer attention. “Our boat is at Wan'an Bridge, Mr Hu. Please come and visit.” Now he understood. Whether her husband came or she did, the purpose was not business: A'zhu wanted to see him. He was willing enough, but could not go immediately. He must avoid arousing his wife's suspicion; besides, having stayed home all morning, he had many affairs to attend to that afternoon. “Certainly. I'll come later today.” “At what time?” “There's much to do. Probably not until sunset.” “Then we'll wait for you to dine.” She rose to leave, adding quietly, “Come early.”

After she had gone, Hu sat lost in thought. He had not expected A'zhu's attachment to be so persistent. Today's visit would evidently involve further complications. He suddenly regretted it. His career had only just begun to advance and needed all his effort. Where would he find spare time for this relationship? Regret was useless. He had promised and could not break his word. Since he must go, he ought to make everyone happy. In his “study” he opened a cupboard containing foreign goods brought from Shanghai as gifts for Wang's official acquaintances. By coincidence, he found several elegant articles intended for Governor Huang's daughter. On returning to Hangzhou, they had learned that she had died of an epidemic illness. The gifts, no longer needed, had remained with Hu. They could now be given to A'zhu.

He wrapped the articles in a cloth bundle and took them out after lunch, visiting the bureau first and Fukang's new premises afterwards. The smell of paint was strong. From front to back, everything was orderly. The rear reception hall had been made splendid enough to impress customers. Yet something still seemed lacking. “Qingsheng, aren't we missing something?” “Paintings and calligraphy.” “Exactly!” Hu was serious. “Those reveal one's standing more than anything. Get them wrong, and they expose you. Don't bring in fakes for connoisseurs to laugh at.” “They won't be false, but the names may be less celebrated.” “Lesser names won't do either. They don't match Fukang's signboard. Tell me whose work you've found.” Liu listed the pieces. Hu was no expert, but knew the relative reputations. He thought only a landscape by Vice Minister Dai Xi—a Hangzhou native now organising militia at home under imperial orders—and a set of four calligraphic panels by Wang Menglou worthy of Fukang. Yet fine works required money and perhaps influence. Liu could not devote himself to the task as though opening an antiques shop rather than a bank. Hu therefore changed to a reassuring, appreciative tone. “Good. We're nearly there. I have some other connections and will find a few more things. You have too much to do. I'll help with the reception room.” Liu understood, but the pleasant wording prevented resentment. “Very well. I'll follow your instructions on the furnishings.”

The discussion and the day were both sufficiently advanced. Hu left Fukang and went directly to Wan'an Bridge. In the eastern city, it was as imposing as Gongchen Bridge at the canal's beginning near the Beixin customs station, and formed the city's principal water landing. Hu left his chair in the bridge lane. People crowded everywhere and masts rose like a forest. He could not tell which boat belonged to the Zhangs. After hesitating, he slowly climbed the stone steps, intending to look out from the top. Halfway up, someone called loudly behind him, “Mr Hu!” He turned to see Old Zhang hurrying up, breathless. “Where's your boat?” “Not here. A'zhu thought it too noisy and told the crew to move it into the city canal. She told me to wait for you at the landing.”
